Where it began

Mark Waugh arrived on 2 June 1965, four minutes behind his twin, Steve, at Canterbury Hospital in the Sydney suburb of Campsie. The boys grew up in Panania, in Sydney's west, and were playing cricket, tennis and soccer in organised teams by the time they were six. Their first cricket match together was not a sign of things to come: both made ducks.

Things improved. In his last year of primary school Mark captained the state's schools sides in both cricket and tennis, and both won national titles. At 17 he made 97 on his first-grade debut for Bankstown, and at 18 he hit 123 for Australia's under-19s at the Adelaide Oval. A younger brother, Dean, later played first-class cricket for New South Wales too.

The player

He had to wait. Steve reached the Test side years earlier, while Mark piled up runs for New South Wales and Essex. In 1990 the twins put on an unbroken 464 together against Western Australia at the WACA, at the time the biggest fifth-wicket stand in first-class history.

His Test chance came at 25, against England at Adelaide in 1991, and he marked it with 138. On the West Indies tour that followed, he and Steve played their first Test side by side, in Trinidad. Mark played 128 Tests, making 8,029 runs at 41.82 with 20 hundreds and a best of 153 not out, and took 59 wickets with medium pace and later off-spin. His 116 in a tense run chase at Port Elizabeth is often picked as his best, and in 1996 he became the first man to make three hundreds at one World Cup. Three years later he won it.

What made him special

Grace, above all. Waugh batted in an unhurried, easy style, with a wonderful gift for working anything on his pads away through the leg side. Against New Zealand at Perth he once drove Daniel Vettori high onto the stand roof, a blow of about 130 metres.

He was also among the finest slip catchers the game has seen. He held 178 catches in Tests, and for a while that was the world record for an outfielder. The ease that made him so lovely to watch did sometimes look a little too relaxed, and the odd soft dismissal was the price. His brother could tell you about the run-outs, too.

Away from the middle

Waugh was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and became a Member of the Order of Australia. After playing he served as a national selector until August 2018, then moved into television commentary with Fox Sports.

And finally

At Lord's in 1993 he reached 99 and looked certain to make a hundred on cricket's most famous ground. Phil Tufnell then bowled one down the leg side that struck his pads and rolled gently back onto the stumps. Four years later he did make a hundred at Lord's, against Middlesex in a tour match. Cricket keeps a few lessons even for the most gifted.
